review_notes: I read the whole file and Height/FiniteOrder.lean, which supplies the general Height.*_iff lemmas that the unit versions specialise. I also checked the Mathlib Height files and DirichletTheorem.logEmbedding_eq_zero_iff for competing simp rules, and the repo's uses of the positivity lemmas. The four @[simp] unit iff lemmas look sound. Their left-hand sides are distinct, and I found no competing simp rules and no loop. The general Height.* lemmas are not simp, so they don't compete. I found nothing for logEmbedding_eq_zero_iff either. The findings below are modest interface gaps and a naming hazard. I did not run Lean, so nothing here has been compiled.

findings.excerpt:
theorem logHeight₁_pos {u : (𝓞 K)ˣ} (hu : u ∉ torsion K) :
    0 < logHeight₁ (u : K) :=
findings.problem: The file makes `= 1` and `= 0` simp-normalise to `u ∈ torsion K`. The strict-inequality counterparts are stated only as one-way implications with an `u ∉ torsion K` hypothesis, and none is tagged simp. So `simp` cannot turn `0 < logHeight₁ (u : K)` or `1 < absMulHeight₁ (u : K)` into `u ∉ torsion K`. Only `=` goals are normalised, so the simp set is incomplete for `<`. A user must apply the lemma by hand and supply the torsion hypothesis. The converse direction, which follows from the existing simp iff lemmas, is not exposed at all.
findings.proposed_change: State the four lemmas as iffs and mark them simp. Examples: `@[simp] theorem logHeight₁_pos_iff (u : (𝓞 K)ˣ) : 0 < logHeight₁ (u : K) ↔ u ∉ torsion K`, and likewise `one_lt_mulHeight₁_iff`, `one_lt_absMulHeight₁_iff` and `absLogHeight₁_pos_iff`. The `→` direction is the current lemma. The `←` direction comes from `lt_of_le_of_ne` together with the existing `*_eq_one_iff` / `*_eq_zero_iff` lemmas, and the nonnegativity facts `one_le_mulHeight₁`, `one_le_absMulHeight₁`, `zero_le_absLogHeight₁`. Keep the implication forms as corollaries, or use `.mpr` at call sites. Termination is fine because the right-hand side is a membership in the torsion subgroup.
findings.benefit: Goals and hypotheses about positive height of units reduce to the same `∈ torsion K` normal form as the equality lemmas. Callers can then use `simp` instead of manually applying `.mpr`/`.mp` with side conditions. The reverse direction (positive height implies nontorsion) also becomes available.

findings.declaration: NumberField.Units.mulHeight₁_eq_one_iff / logHeight₁_eq_zero_iff / absMulHeight₁_eq_one_iff / absLogHeight₁_eq_zero_iff (simp lemmas sharing names with Height.* and NumberField.* lemmas)
findings.excerpt:
theorem logHeight₁_eq_zero_iff (u : (𝓞 K)ˣ) :
    logHeight₁ (u : K) = 0 ↔ u ∈ torsion K := by
findings.problem: These simp lemmas reuse the short names of the general lemmas `Height.mulHeight₁_eq_one_iff`, `Height.logHeight₁_eq_zero_iff`, `NumberField.absMulHeight₁_eq_one_iff` and `NumberField.absLogHeight₁_eq_zero_iff`. The file does `open Height NumberField`, and downstream files also use the same names. Inside the file, the general lemmas must be written with full qualification, and unqualified `rw [logHeight₁_eq_zero_iff, ...]` (line 73) and `(mulHeight₁_eq_one_iff u).mp` (line 79) rely on overload resolution. A user who writes `simp [logHeight₁_eq_zero_iff]` under `open Height` in a unit context risks an ambiguous-overload error or picks the wrong lemma. The wrong one carries an `x = 0 ∨ IsOfFinOrder x` shape and Northcott or integrality side requirements. For a simp interface, the unit lemmas should be unambiguously nameable.
findings.proposed_change: Rename the unit simp lemmas so they are distinguishable, for example `Units.mulHeight₁_coe_eq_one_iff`, `Units.logHeight₁_coe_eq_zero_iff` and so on. Alternatively, keep the names but drop `open Height`/`open NumberField` and qualify the general lemmas everywhere. Update the internal uses at lines 73 and 79 accordingly.
findings.benefit: `simp [name]` and `rw [name]` resolve unambiguously to the intended unit-specific normal-form lemma. Readers can see which of the two competing statements (the general `x = 0 ∨ IsOfFinOrder x` form or the unit `∈ torsion` form) is being used.
